questions.stem: Rule by the wealthy is called:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'ploutos' = wealth (Pluto = god of wealth/underworld). All four distractors are same-family, so the student must know the whole cluster.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Rule by religious authority is called:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'theos' = god. Theocracy = government by priestly or religious class. Historically: Vatican City; Iran under vilayat-e-faqih.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Rule by the elderly is called:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'geron' = old man (also root of 'geriatrics', 'gerontology'). Gerontocracy recurs in editorials on political systems.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Rule by a few (a small group) is called:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'oligos' = few. Monarchy = one; democracy = the people; anarchy = no rule. Oligarchy is the structural counterpart of the others.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Rule by technical experts is called:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'techne' = craft, skill. Technocracy is a government run by technical specialists. Often contrasted with democracy in policy debates.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Rule by the worst citizens is called:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'kakistos' = worst (superlative of 'kakos'). A rare but editor-loved word. Ochlocracy = mob rule; kleptocracy = thieves rule.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: A state of no rule / no government is called:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'an-' (without) + 'arche' (rule). Colloquially means chaos; in political theory, rule of self-governing communities without hierarchical state.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Rule based on ability and talent is called:
questions.explanation: L. 'meritum' = reward. Term popularised by Michael Young (1958) satirically; now used neutrally. High-hit in UPSC / editorials.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Rule by the 'best' or noble-born is called:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'aristos' = best (originally 'best-born', nobility). Over time acquired the class/pedigree meaning. Distinguished from meritocracy, where 'best' is earned, not inherited.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Rule by officials and desk-based administrators is called:
questions.explanation: Fr. 'bureau' = writing desk / office + Gk. '-cracy'. Bureaucracy therefore = rule by the desk / office holders. Coined by Vincent de Gournay (1745). Often pejorative today.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: A country where the armed forces hold supreme authority over the civilian government is said to be governed by?

options.option_text: Ochlocracy — rule exercised by an unruly mob or crowd
Stratocracy — rule exercised directly by the military
Plutocracy — rule exercised by the wealthiest citizens
Meritocracy — rule exercised by the most talented individuals

questions.explanation: Stratocracy (Greek: stratos = army) is the term for military-run government. Plutocracy (wealth) and Meritocracy (merit) are common distractors but refer to wealth and talent respectively. Ochlocracy means mob rule, entirely unrelated to armed forces.

questions.stem: Autocracy and Monarchy both involve a single ruler, yet differ in the origin of authority. Which option correctly distinguishes Monarchy from Autocracy?

options.option_text: Monarchy — a single ruler who seized power by conquest or coup
Autocracy — a single ruler whose powers are limited by constitution
Monarchy — a single hereditary sovereign whose title passes by birth
Autocracy — rule shared jointly between two hereditary co-rulers

questions.explanation: Monarchy (Greek: monos = alone, archein = rule) specifically denotes hereditary succession. Autocracy (autos = self) denotes absolute personal power regardless of how it was acquired — a monarch can be autocratic, but not all autocrats are monarchs. Option A inverts the definition, and Option B wrongly adds constitutional limits to autocracy.

questions.stem: When established institutions collapse and policy is dictated by an impassioned, unruly crowd rather than elected representatives, the resulting system is termed?

options.option_text: Pantisocracy — an ideal of equal governance shared by all citizens
Ethnocracy — governance dominated by a single ethnic or racial group
Ochlocracy — governance by a volatile and uncontrollable mob
Nomocracy — governance bound strictly by a codified written law

questions.explanation: Ochlocracy (Greek: ochlos = mob) is the classical term for mob rule, identified by Polybius as the degenerate form of democracy. Pantisocracy (equal rule by all) is the utopian ideal — its opposite. Nomocracy (nomos = law) means rule of law, the very thing ochlocracy destroys, making it a plausible-but-wrong distractor.

questions.stem: Derived from the Greek word for 'thief', which term describes a political system where rulers systematically loot the state treasury for personal enrichment?

options.option_text: Kakistocracy — governance by those least qualified or most unfit
Kleptocracy — governance by rulers who pillage public resources
Ethnocracy — governance by a dominant racial or ethnic community
Plutocracy — governance by those who already hold the most wealth

questions.explanation: Kleptocracy (Greek: kleptes = thief) literally means 'rule by thieves' and describes corrupt regimes that plunder national resources. Kakistocracy (kakistos = worst) is the strongest distractor since corrupt rulers often are unfit, but the etymology — and the emphasis on stealing — points unambiguously to kleptocracy. Plutocracy implies inherited or earned wealth, not theft.

questions.stem: In anthropology, the term for a social system in which mothers or the eldest female lineage members hold primary authority over family, clan, and property is?

options.option_text: Gynarchy — political rule exercised exclusively by women leaders
Matriarchy — authority vested in mothers or senior female lineage
Androcracy — political domination exercised by men over all women
Patriarchy — authority vested in fathers or the senior male lineage

questions.explanation: Matriarchy (Latin: mater = mother) refers to lineage-based authority held by mothers or female elders in social/familial units. Gynarchy (gyne = woman) is the strongest distractor — it means political rule by women broadly, whereas matriarchy is specifically about maternal lineage authority in kin-based societies. Patriarchy is the male counterpart, useful as a contrastive distractor.

questions.stem: Plato, in the 'Republic', described a polity where civic rights and eligibility for office are calibrated to the amount of property a citizen owns. He called this form?

options.option_text: Kritarchy — governance exercised through judges who interpret law
Timocracy — governance where rights are proportional to property
Ergatocracy — governance by an organised industrial working class
Squirearchy — governance dominated by the rural landowning gentry

questions.explanation: Timocracy (Greek: timē = honour/value/property) in Plato's usage links civic standing directly to property ownership — distinct from aristocracy (birth) or meritocracy (ability). Squirearchy is the strongest distractor since it also involves land and property, but squirearchy is a sociological label for British gentry dominance, not a Platonic constitutional category. Kritarchy and Ergatocracy operate on wholly different axes.

questions.stem: Biblical Israel during the period of the 'Judges' had no monarch and no legislature — only magistrate-judges who ruled by interpreting divine law. What is the technical term for this system?

options.option_text: Nomocracy — strict governance by a codified body of secular law
Theocracy — governance directed by ordained religious clergy leaders
Kritarchy — governance solely by judges with no other ruling branch
Hagiarchy — governance by a formal council of saints or holy persons

questions.explanation: Kritarchy (Greek: krites = judge) describes government exclusively by judges — no separate executive or legislature. Biblical Israel under the Judges (Book of Judges) is the textbook example. Theocracy is the strongest distractor: the judges did interpret divine law, but theocracy implies a priestly class governing in God's name, not judicial figures empowered by personal authority. Hagiarchy (saints) and Nomocracy (written secular law) do not fit the judicial-only structure.
